subject: AI & Agents
title: Labels and Supervision
description: A micro-lesson that makes Labels and Supervision usable.

hook.text: A child learns 'dog' because someone points at a dog and says 'dog.' Labels work the same way.

buildup.text: In supervised learning, each training example comes paired with the correct answer — the label.

discovery.text: Labels can be categories ('cat' or 'dog') or numbers (house price: $350,000).

twist.text: Labeling data is expensive. ImageNet required 25,000 workers to label 14 million images.

climax.text: The quality of labels directly determines the quality of the model. Garbage labels, garbage model.

punchline.text: AI learns from answers. The answers better be right.

quiz.question: What is a label in supervised learning?
options: The correct answer paired with each training example

details.summary: Labels are the correct answers attached to training examples — labeling a photo as 'cat' or an email as 'spam.' These labels teach the model what to look for during supervised learning.
details.whyItMatters: Label quality determines model quality. Incorrect, inconsistent, or biased labels produce unreliable AI. Understanding labeling reveals a hidden human workforce behind every AI system.
takeaways: Labels are correct answers paired with training inputs
They guide the model to learn specific patterns and categories
Label quality directly impacts model accuracy and fairness

faq.question: Who creates the labels for AI training data?
faq.answer: Large-scale labeling is done by human annotators, often through platforms like Amazon Mechanical Turk or specialized data labeling companies. Expert domains like medicine require trained professionals.

faq.question: What happens when labels are wrong?
faq.answer: The model learns incorrect patterns. If 10% of cat images are mislabeled as dogs, the model's accuracy ceiling drops. Large-scale mislabeling can systematically bias the model's outputs.
